scenes.narration: Three point six nine cents. That is what it cost the United States Mint to make a single one-cent coin, in its twenty twenty-four fiscal year.
So every new penny was a small loss. Add them up, and in that one year the Mint spent eighty-five point three million dollars more making pennies than the pennies were worth.
So why did it take so long to stop? And what happens to your change now?
By the end of this video, you will know how a coin ends up costing more than it is worth, how stores round your change without it, and why the nickel may be next.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Governments usually make money on coins. A quarter costs much less than twenty-five cents to make, so every quarter the Mint ships is a small profit. Economists call that profit seigniorage. In twenty twenty-four, quarters alone earned the Mint one hundred and sixty-five point six million dollars.

The penny went the other way. Its cost jumped about twenty percent in one year, from about three cents to three point six nine cents. According to the Treasury, it was only around one point three cents a decade earlier. The Mint shipped more than three billion new pennies in twenty twenty-four, and every one of them lost money.

Here is another way to see it. For every one dollar of pennies the Mint sent out, it spent about two dollars and sixty-nine cents more than that dollar was worth. A dime costs under six cents to make. A quarter, under fifteen. Those coins pay their way. The penny never could.

And it was not a one-year accident. The Mint reports that both the penny and the nickel have cost more than their face value for nineteen fiscal years in a row. The nickel, worth five cents, cost thirteen point seven eight cents to make.

Across all circulating coins, the Mint still made a profit, about ninety-nine point five million dollars in twenty twenty-four. But that was sixty percent less than the year before. The losing coins were eating into the winners.

Let me draw the coin ledger. Here is the quarter, a big profit bar. The dime, a smaller profit. Then below the line, the nickel, a loss. And the penny, the biggest loss of all. Two coins pay for themselves. Two coins cost the government money every time they are made.

scenes.narration: For years, that loss was simply accepted. Then, in twenty twenty-five, the government finally pulled the plug.

keyframes.label: For years, the loss was accepted…

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: On November twelfth, twenty twenty-five, in Philadelphia, the Mint held a ceremonial strike of the final circulating penny. The Treasurer of the United States pressed the button. According to the St. Louis Fed, it ended two hundred and thirty-two years of penny production.

keyframes.cue: According to the St. Louis Fed
keyframes.label: cam[1].at.cue

scenes.narration: In practice, the flow had stopped even earlier. According to the Federal Reserve, it received its last new pennies from the Mint shortly after May twenty twenty-five, months before the ceremony.

But the penny did not disappear. It is still legal tender. The Mint keeps making a few for collectors. And the Federal Reserve keeps moving the old ones around. Its banks resumed taking penny deposits in January twenty twenty-six, and today every one of its coin terminals fills penny orders again.

How many pennies are out there? Nobody knows exactly. The Treasury talks about roughly one hundred and fourteen billion. The Mint has estimated three hundred billion in circulation. Either way, far more than the Mint says commerce needs. The Treasury says the Federal Reserve will keep recirculating the existing pennies for as long as possible.

Stopping production saves money. According to the Treasury, about fifty-six million dollars a year in materials alone. That is small for the federal budget, but it ends a loss that grew every year the coin got more expensive to make.

Let me draw the penny's journey. Here is the Mint, where new pennies used to start. Then the Fed, then the banks, then the stores, then your pocket, and often a jar. Now the first step is gone. The coins still circulate, but no new ones come in to replace those that vanish into jars.

keyframes.cue: Now the first step is gone
keyframes.label: strokes[7].start.cue

scenes.narration: Which leaves a very practical question. What happens at the cash register when the pennies run out?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The Treasury published guidance, not a law. It only applies to cash, and only to the final total, after tax. If the total ends in one, two, six or seven cents, round down. If it ends in three, four, eight or nine, round up to the nearest five.

keyframes.cue: If the total ends in one
keyframes.label: cam[1].at.cue

scenes.narration: So a bill of four dollars and ninety-eight cents becomes five dollars. But a bill of four dollars and ninety-six cents becomes four ninety-five. If you pay by card, nothing changes at all. You still pay to the exact cent. And the rounding happens once, on the whole receipt, not on every item in your basket. A cart of fifty items gets rounded one time, at the end.

States are writing their own rules. Washington passed a law in twenty twenty-six that lets stores round cash payments the same way, but does not force them to. It took effect in June. Customers can still pay with exact change, and tax is added before any rounding. In Congress, the House and the Senate each passed their own version of a rounding bill, called the Common Cents Act, in twenty twenty-six. As of August, they had not agreed on one text, so it is not law yet.

Does rounding cheat shoppers? The Richmond Fed studied it. Its researchers estimate the cost to consumers at about six million dollars a year, across the whole country. By our calculation, that is less than two cents per American, per year.

Let me draw the rounding wheel. Here are the last digits, zero to nine. One and two go down to zero. Three and four go up to five. Six and seven go down to five. Eight and nine go up to the next ten. Half the time you win a cent or two. Half the time you lose one.

scenes.narration: This is not the first time America has had to rethink the penny. And it is not the first country to drop one.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: In nineteen eighty-two, the Mint changed the recipe to save money. The penny went from ninety-five percent copper to almost ninety-eight percent zinc, with only a little copper. At the time, the change was expected to save the Treasury around twenty-five million dollars a year.

Canada went further. In May twenty twelve, its finance minister struck the country's last penny in Winnipeg. Its mint stopped sending pennies to banks in February twenty thirteen. Each one cost about one point six cents Canadian cents to make.

The government expected to save eleven million Canadian dollars a year. At the exchange rate of January twenty thirteen, that is about eleven million US dollars. Canadians have rounded their cash payments ever since.

Let me draw the timeline. Nineteen eighty-two, the copper penny becomes a zinc penny. Twenty thirteen, Canada stops handing out pennies. Twenty twenty-five, the United States strikes its last one. Each time, the same reason. The metal cost more than the coin.

scenes.visual_objective: Kinetic typography: lines enter word by word on narration cues
scenes.narration: And that same reason is now staring at the next coin up.

keyframes.label: …is staring at the next coin up

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: The nickel is a bigger loss per coin than the penny ever was. In twenty twenty-four it cost almost fourteen cents to make a five-cent coin. The Mint lost about seventeen point seven million dollars on nickels that year, less in total than on pennies.

But dropping the nickel would be harder. Without pennies and nickels, cash would round to the nearest ten cents. The Richmond Fed estimates that would cost consumers about about fifty-six million dollars a year, nearly ten times the cost of rounding to five cents.

There is also a bigger trend behind all of this. According to the St. Louis Fed, cash was used in only about fourteen percent of payments in twenty twenty-four. Every year, fewer people need small coins at all. That makes it easier for governments to stop making them. For the Mint, ending the penny means less zinc and copper to buy, fewer coins to strike, and one less loss on its books every single year. For shoppers, it mostly means a slightly different number at the cash register.

scenes.narration: Let me draw the trade-off. On one side, the cost of making coins that lose money. On the other side, the cost of rounding without them. For the penny, the minting loss was far bigger than the rounding cost. For the nickel, by these estimates, rounding would cost more than the minting loss. That is one reason the nickel is a harder call.

So why did America stop making the penny? Because a coin is not just money. It is a product, made of metal, with a cost. When the cost of the product rises above the value printed on it, every new coin is a loss. The penny crossed that line years ago. The only surprise is how long it took to stop.
